first_impression.reaction: Okay, the first line answers me straight away: it's several events, not one night, and it lists them. The second paragraph is mostly the site talking about its sources, which I skimmed past, but Key Takeaways come right after so I didn't have to scroll much. The title is a bit clickbait though: 'You Did Not Know' is a weird promise for someone who knows nothing yet.

journey.quote: It is a sequence: a family visit to ask, nights of singing, a henna gathering, a march with drums, a line of dancers stamping in time.
journey.reaction: This is the answer in one sentence. Good, I've basically got it already on the train.

journey.quote: This guide follows the order of a real celebration and traces each meaning to UNESCO, museum dress collections and named reference works.
journey.reaction: Fine, but it's the site explaining itself. I'd rather go straight to the list. It's short so it didn't lose me.

journey.quote: UNESCO lists Palestinian embroidery (2021) and dabkeh (2023), and in 2024 added henna as an element shared by several countries.
journey.reaction: Dated and specific. This is the kind of thing that makes me trust a page and maybe bookmark it.

journey.quote: Smartraveller advises Australians not to travel to Palestine, so couples bring these customs to a wedding at home or elsewhere, with space planned for the zaffeh, dabke and henna night.
journey.reaction: Slightly odd in a takeaways list when I just asked what the traditions are, and I'm not Australian. It's useful context but it's not the answer to my question, and the words zaffeh and dabke haven't been explained yet at this point.
Headings follow the order of events and each custom has its own name as a subheading. Very easy to scan on a phone.

journey.quote: For Muslim families, the religious marriage is the katb al-kitab, the signing of the Islamic marriage contract, often held before the larger celebration.
journey.reaction: Feels thin compared to the other sections. One sentence, then it sends me to another guide. Not a big deal.

journey.quote: A Glasgow Museums curator notes that despite many attempts to give motifs symbolic meaning, the patterns generally had no special meanings, though embroiderers named them to tell them apart.
journey.reaction: Actually interesting, and it's the one 'did not know' moment the title promised. Other sites would just invent meanings.

journey.quote: During the sahra, the groom is shaved in public, in front of the guests, by his family, while everyone cheers and sings.
journey.reaction: Fun detail, but the heading says 'groom's shave' and the section starts by explaining the sahra. Slightly backwards; I had to read twice to see where the sahra was introduced.

journey.quote: Dress for a long evening on your feet: you will very likely be pulled into a dabke line.
journey.reaction: Practical for me if I'm a guest. The FAQ answers the obvious follow-up questions quickly.

unanswered_questions: What dishes are usually served? The page deliberately doesn't list any, which is honest but leaves me without an example.
What actually happens at a Palestinian Christian church wedding? The page says its sources don't cover it.
Is there a rough running order or timeline for a typical diaspora wedding weekend (which night is which)?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Palestinian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Clickbait-style title. I searched a plain question; a plain title like 'Palestinian Wedding Traditions: A Guide' would match it better.

turn_offs_found.quote: Where a story is only "often told", we say so.
turn_offs_found.why: Meta talk about the method in the intro, before the answer list. Small, but it's the only bit of fluff before the takeaways.

would_share_with: A friend going to a Palestinian wedding as a guest (for the FAQ and dabke bits)

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like help shaping these evenings into one plan, speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: I'm only here for information, not planning a wedding. The magazine link is the one I might tap if anything. The CTA isn't pushy, so it didn't annoy me.

top_3_changes: Swap the 'You Did Not Know' title for a plain one that matches the search, e.g. 'Palestinian Wedding Traditions: Customs, Meanings and Order of Events'.

Make the first takeaway a quick one-line list of the main customs in order (tulbeh, sahra, henna night, zaffeh, dabke, feast) and move the Smartraveller point lower, so the takeaways answer the query first.
In 'The groom's shave', lead with the shave and introduce the sahra in its own line or subheading so the heading matches the first sentence.
